title: What Does 4QM Assessment Look Like?
author: J.B. Bassett
summary: Bassett answers a question the Four Question Method team fields constantly: what a 4QM unit test actually looks like. His answer is that the test looks like the teaching, because the same four moves students rehearse in class, narration, interpretation, explanation and judgment, are the moves the test asks them to make without their notes. He concedes that multiple choice is a legitimate and efficient format, then argues it can only test recall of someone else's answers rather than a student's own capacity to narrate or interpret, which is why the U.S. History assessments now being written require handwritten prose. The piece walks through the mechanics question by question: a unit-level narrative built from a supplied list of fifteen people, events and ideas, a short primary source excerpt to contextualize and interpret, and for the harder Questions Three and Four either a recap of the class conclusion or an application of the class thinking to an unfamiliar case. Difficulty is tuned by small design choices, such as sorting the narrative list alphabetically rather than chronologically, or supplying a document students have never seen. Bassett closes with his own classroom practice, cutting sections when the load got heavy while keeping the constraint that students write enough for him to judge both knowledge and skill.
points: Because the storyboard and unit guide govern instruction all unit long, they convert directly into review tools, so preparing for the test and reviewing the content become the same act.
The Question One task supplies fifteen key people, events and ideas and requires at least ten of them in a written unit narrative scored for change over time, active voice, coherence and accuracy.
Sorting the item list alphabetically instead of chronologically is offered as the lever that makes the narrative task harder, a rare case of difficulty being designed rather than discovered.
For Questions Three and Four, letting students consult the lesson templates they built in class is what makes it fair to hold them to a high standard on an unfamiliar case.
Multiple choice is not rejected as invalid, only as unable to make student thinking visible, which is the stated purpose of assessment here.
quotes: One of the things we love about the Four Question Method is that there’s no real difference between what happens in class and what happens on the test.

4QM unit tests require students to do exactly the same thing, only without consulting their notes. The unit storyboard and unit guide define instruction during the unit, and become test review tools at the end.
Those questions would certainly test students’ recall of the answers, but almost certainly would not test their own ability to narrate, interpret, explain, or judge.

We recommend that every unit test require students to write a unit-level narrative. A great way to do this is to provide a list of fifteen key people, events, and ideas from the unit, and require students to write the story of the unit while including at least ten items from the list.

We recommend that every unit test require students to interpret a short excerpt from a primary source document or an artifact of some kind. This task requires students to go through the same steps as a Question Two interpretation lesson: contextualize the document or artifact by situating it in the unit story, describe its plain meaning, then interpret the author’s purpose and assumptions.
The second option is to allow students to refer to the lesson templates they completed in class, and to ask them to apply their thinking to a new case.
When I was still a classroom teacher, students often asked me, “Mr. Bassett, what’s gonna be on the unit test?” I would always respond, “There are only four questions I can ask you in this class.
